introduction: The Persian word tadbír means management, forethought, tact. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s letters are full of it, down to how tea should be made and that letters should be numbered; and Shoghi Effendi and the Universal House of Justice add the counterweight, that administration “is to be conceived as an instrument and not a substitute”, to be kept flexible and free of needless rules. The guide follows both. Proverbs is the Bible’s handbook of prudence, and the Gospels have the tower-builder who counts the cost and “wise as serpents”. Aristotle’s mean and his “right person … right time”, Franklin’s struggle with Order, and Herbert’s room swept “as for Thy laws” belong with the first half. For the second, there are “the sabbath was made for man”, new wine and old bottles, Lao Tzu’s water, Emerson and Burke. Hamlet and Confucius’s “twice may do” speak against overthinking, and the Sermon on the Mount against too careful a guard of one’s rights.
questions: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá cared how tea was served and letters numbered. What is the spiritual significance of small order?
When does deliberation become Hamlet’s “pale cast of thought”? How does one know it is time to act?
Readings 40 to 49 warn against rules multiplying. Why do communities make them, and what is lost?
“Uniformity in principle, diversity in detail.” Give an example of each from a community you know.
Reading 27 says not to yield a dollar wrongfully taken; Jesus says to turn the other cheek. Is there a way to honour both?

outside.why: Without organization even a household is in confusion. Let all things be done decently and in order.
Deliberation is essential before action. Which of you, intending to build a tower, sitteth not down first, and counteth the cost?

Hamlet knew what too much deliberation does: the native hue of resolution is sicklied o’er with the pale cast of thought, and enterprises of great pith and moment lose the name of action. Where is the line between prudence and paralysis?
Told of a man who thought three times before acting, Confucius said: twice may do.
Be moderate in all affairs. Virtue is a state of character lying in a mean.
Governments acting without thought of consequences. A prudent man foreseeth the evil, and hideth himself: but the simple pass on, and are punished.
Whatever is undertaken should be done with thoroughness and order. Whatsoever thy hand findeth to do, do it with thy might.
In no matter let go of wisdom. Be ye therefore wise as serpents, and harmless as doves.
Man should not act on his own thought alone. Without counsel purposes are disappointed.
“Be not the slave of your moods, but their master.” He that ruleth his spirit is better than he that taketh a city.
A lecturer prepares; so should every undertaking. Ponder the path of thy feet, and let all thy ways be established.
The home should be orderly. Franklin made a method of it: I conceived the bold and arduous project of arriving at moral perfection.
Tea must be made properly or not at all. Herbert: who sweeps a room as for Thy laws, makes that and the action fine.
Be thoughtful about the work and make preparations. Go to the ant, thou sluggard; she provideth her meat in the summer.
Number the letters, so you know which arrived. He that is faithful in that which is least is faithful also in much.
However perfect the organization, negligence undoes it. What I say unto you I say unto all, Watch.
Without the power of religion it will end in assemblies and speeches. If ye give them not those things which are needful; what doth it profit?

Give a thousand freely, but yield not a dollar to one who would take it wrongfully. Jesus: resist not evil: but whosoever shall smite thee on thy right cheek, turn to him the other also. How do you reconcile the reading with the saying?
Moderation; consider the taste of the public. Let your speech be always with grace, seasoned with salt.

Send the books one at a time. Aristotle: to do this to the right person, to the right extent, at the right time, with the right motive, and in the right way, that is not for every one, nor is it easy.
Leave it unspoken for the present. A time to keep silence, and a time to speak.
This year or next, whenever wisdom requires. To every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven.
Once decided, nothing hindered them. There is a tide in the affairs of men, which, taken at the flood, leads on to fortune.
“God loveth the ordering of all things.” Lo! We have created every thing by measure.
Administration is an instrument and not a substitute for the Faith. The sabbath was made for man, and not man for the sabbath.
Do not lay down a fixed pattern for future society before its time. Take therefore no thought for the morrow: for the morrow shall take thought for the things of itself.
Uniformity in principle, diversity in detail. Emerson: a foolish consistency is the hobgoblin of little minds.
Keep the administration as flexible as possible. Lao Tzu: the highest excellence is like that of water.
No uniform ritual is to be imposed. The letter killeth, but the spirit giveth life.
The tendency to pour the Faith into moulds. Neither do men put new wine into old bottles.
New rules and regulations. They bind heavy burdens and grievous to be borne.
Change is constant, and procedures must change with it. Burke: a state without the means of some change is without the means of its conservation.
